I'd just like to first say that /u/Atko and team have been doing an amazing job keeping this site up and running...even as a former web dev, I have no idea how they're doing this. Thanks a lot guys, this is now one of the best platforms on the internet to share and find content!

Nevertheless, the future of this website needs to be planned, and reddit-style breakdowns need to be avoided. There were multiple issues on reddit:

  1. Admins monetizing reddit in ways detrimental to the society

  2. Mods not being given tools to adequately keep up subreddit quality, while being given some tools that give them too much control over subreddit content

  3. Users posting low-quality content which gets upvoted at the cost of controversial high-quality posts

All three points can be resolved by understanding that these kinds of online communites have very high user mobility, so in digg, reddit, Voat, etc, the user is the king. In comparison, Facebook relies on people's friends to keep them locked into their system, while Twitter acts as a real-time news stream, which makes competition difficult because of the critical mass of users needed to keep things updated all the time. Users are effectively locked into using Fb/Twitter for these functions, but in the case of digg/reddit/Voat-like content aggregation websites, it is easy to move to a new site.

So for the above three points, this is what we could do:

  1. Admins have to find ways to monetize that don't kill multiple online communities...the recent posts by the Voat admins about

  2. Mods need to serve the users. They have to be given powerful tools that allow them to give users a good experience, while keeping any tools that have abuse-potential (like shadowbans and post-deletion) transparent and open to criticism; some of this is already on Voat, which makes me really happy. The mods need to be responsible to someone...either the community (via referendum/voating on moderator positions), or the admins (via some meta-Voat community). I know that moderating is a difficult, thankless job, but shouldn't there be a way to remove dangerous/cancerous/power-mad mods?

  3. Users have to be listened to, so that some kind of absurd internet uprising doesn't happen on Voat due to out-of-touch admins. I know that this is difficult for /u/Atko and team with their current workload, but could we have an hourlong weekly "State of the Voat Union" thread, in which users get to interact with site admins and mods?
What's been happening at reddit is a disgrace to all online communities. Could we discuss ways to avoid this from happening on Voat?

Honestly I think the admins are already very active with the users, all of the issues raised by people on various subs seem to be given attention. I've made two posts asking about problems with the site and both of them were answered by Atko quite quickly. I really don't think there's anything that can be done about users posting low quality content though, it seems to be a symptom of having a site with a large amount of users. The only thing that might help is if moderators made more rules on their subs and enforced them by taking down unrelated posts.

I think the partner program is a very unique and potentially awesome idea (https://voat.co/p/partnerprogram). In short, the partner program is a monetary rewards program for a select number of users/mods. I do have some mixed feelings about this, however. Should Voat go the same way as Reddit, will the fact that a large number of users/mods are sharing in the profits dampen the outcry i.e. are we being payed off? Will some kind of hierarchy be established as far as whose concerns are attended to?

Honestly, I'm conflicted about this. I dislike the idea that commenters could get treated as second class contributors if only mods and selected posters are partners. Every comment written is a contribution, and the comments are often more interesting than the linked content.

I think the key to avoiding another digg/slashdot/myspace/reddit is to listen to the users, not shareholders. The users know what's wrong with the site. They are also willing to put lots of free work into the site (contributing, moderating, creating content, commenting, writing tools...).

As for monetization, I don't think any user has a problem with that, just don't expect to become a billionaire with a site, just see it as a normal job. Venture capital is probably problematic in that regard. If at some point you decide that you need a "cleaner" appearance for the masses, I don't think that would be very controversial.. Just change whatever is visible in /v/all, don't kill off popular or controversial subs that appear there, and maybe make /v/unfiltered.

Oh, and less shadowbanning, lies, doublespeak, etc..

If you're concerned about moderator abuse, I came up with a system that would help combat the issue: /v/thesystem. If you're at all interested.

It allows the users to have control over who's moderating the site and is, as another user put it, "a system of self-governed quadruple redundancy checks and balances."

It relies on the userbase and requires absolutely no admin intervention. The only thing admins would have to do is put this system in place on the site (i.e. code it in).
